Article Title: Urine biomarker may offer new way to flag cancer risk in India, study suggests
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With an estimated 15.6 lakh new cancer cases and 8.7 lakh deaths in India in 2024, a new study points to a possible way of identifying people at higher risk of developing cancer even before symptoms appear: a urine biomarker.The research, published in Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention last week, found that the profile of certain molecules in urine could help predict the risk of developing multiple cancers over five years.The study followed healthy adults enrolled in the Lifelines population cohort in the Netherlands. Researchers analysed 24-hour urine samples from all 827 participants who developed cancer within five years and a random sample of 4,609 who did not. The results were scaled to estimate risk across a cohort of 1,24,436 adults.Researchers from Lund University, the University of Liverpool, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Elypta measured three chondroitin sulphate disaccharides in urine using mass spectrometry. They combined these measurements into a GAGome score and assessed its predictive value both independently and alongside 13 established risk factors.The five-year risk of developing cancer was 0.18% in the low-risk group, 2.3% in the intermediate-risk group, 7.6% in the high-risk group and 32% in the very-high-risk group. A one standard deviation increase in the score was associated with a 66% higher risk of cancer, even after accounting for established risk factors.The researchers estimated that screening people classified as high risk could identify 54% of cancers, including 54% of in-situ carcinomas, with a 17% false-positive rate.“The association was independent of established risk factors and consistent across cancer stages, which makes this dynamic biological marker worth testing prospectively,” said John Field, professor of molecular oncology at the University of Liverpool and a co-author of the study.“Urinary GAG profiling offers a promising, non-invasive approach to identifying people at increased risk of multiple cancers. However, findings from the Dutch population cannot be directly extrapolated to India because of differences in genetic backgrounds, risk factors and cancer patterns. Large, multicentric studies in Indian populations are needed to establish its accuracy and cost-effectiveness. The test should be considered for wider screening only if it demonstrates improved early diagnosis and reduced cancer mortality,” said Dr Abhishek Shankar, associate professor of radiation oncology at AIIMS.The findings could pave the way for more personalised cancer risk assessment, but the urine biomarker is not a diagnostic test. Its accuracy and clinical usefulness will need to be established through further prospective studies, particularly in Indian populations, before it can be considered for wider screening.
Article Summary: A new study points to a possible way of identifying people at higher risk of developing cancer even before symptoms appear. The study followed healthy adults enrolled in the Lifelines population cohort in the Netherlands. Researchers analysed 24-hour urine samples from all 827 participants who developed cancer within five years.

NEW DELHI: Central consumer protection authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of Rs 10 lakh on ANI Technologies, which operates ride-hailing platform Ola , for misleading consumers into paying an additional fare to improve their chances of getting a faster ride.It has also directed the platform to immediately discontinue display of all prompts, messages, interface designs, pre-set amounts, or any other dark pattern elements that “solicit, nudge, coerce or psychologically pressure consumers into paying any amount, whether described as a tip, add-on, additional fare or by any other name, over and above the upfront fare displayed at the time of booking, prior to the completion of the journey”.The action follows a similar order and Rs 10 lakh penalty in Sep against ride-hailing platform Rapido for a similar violation. CCPA had also ordered Rapido to discontinue this practice. TOI has learnt that CCPA is also investigating similar complaints against another popular ride-hailing platform.The penalty so far seems to have had little impact as such platforms are continuing the practice.The authority took up a complaint it received in May 2025 alleging that Ola’s app was prompting customers to pay tips in advance out of fear that their bookings could be delayed or drivers might not accept their rides.The app displayed the message, “adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster”, along with pre-set tip amounts.Ola had defended this, saying that it only offered customers an option to voluntarily reward drivers and the entire tip went to them. The company also argued that ride allocation and driver acceptance were determined by standardised algorithms that did not take tipping behaviour into account. It maintained that customers had equal access to rides irrespective of whether they chose to pay an additional amount.The company had also told the authority that it had modified the user interface, presenting the payment as an optional add-on. However, the CCPA observed that Ola had not provided technical evidence or backend documentation to substantiate its claim that tipping did not influence ride allocation.The regulator said suggesting that an additional payment could improve the chances of securing a quicker ride could create a misleading impression among consumers and undermine the voluntary nature of tipping. It also said that consumers should not be made to feel that they need to pay over and above the disclosed fare to receive a basic service.
